paragraphs: This paper asks how much additional depth a transformer needs as its input grows. Earlier theoretical limits typically hold the number of layers constant, making it difficult to distinguish an absolute architectural barrier from a restriction caused by keeping depth fixed. The authors instead study transformers whose depth grows logarithmically with context length.

They show that this modest growth allows even highly uniform transformers to recognize regular languages and determine graph connectivity. These tasks capture state tracking and reasoning through connected steps. Under standard complexity conjectures, fixed-depth transformers cannot express either problem. The analysis also quantifies depth requirements and finds depth scaling more efficient than increasing width or adding chain-of-thought steps for these problems.

The experiments examine whether this expressive capacity can actually be learned. For regular language recognition, the theoretical depth requirements closely match the depth needed for successful training. That agreement connects a mathematical account of representational power to practical architecture selection, while keeping the empirical finding tied to the particular task studied.
neurips-2025-a-little-depth-goes-a-long-.tldr: Logarithmically increasing transformer depth enables important sequential reasoning tasks, with predicted depth requirements matching training results for regular language recognition.

paragraphs: Astronomical observations come in heterogeneous forms, creating a need for models that can learn relationships across different kinds of data. AION-1 addresses that need with a family of foundation models designed for joint astronomical modeling. Its central aim is to support transformations between data types within a unified framework.

The architecture has two stages. First, a tokenizer specific to each modality converts its observations into tokens. A transformer then performs masked modeling over sequences containing tokens from different modalities. This separates the handling of each data type from the shared task of learning relationships across observations, giving the model a common framework for cross-modal prediction.

Trained on more than 200 million astronomical objects, AION-1 shows strong performance in numerical prediction, classification, generation, and object retrieval. The breadth of these tasks supports the authors' proposal that joint modeling can serve multiple scientific uses. They also present the design as a scalable blueprint for other scientific domains and release the dataset, training script, and model weights as open source.
neurips-2025-aion-1-omnimodal-foundation.tldr: AION-1 uses modality-specific tokenization and shared transformer modeling to support diverse astronomical prediction, generation, and retrieval tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the distribution produced by a diffusion model changes during training. The authors develop exact mathematical solutions for gradient-flow training in one- or two-layer linear denoisers, including linear convolutional versions, with arbitrary data. These settings make it possible to connect changes in model weights directly to changes in generated outputs.

Using the Gaussian equivalence principle, the analysis follows learning along principal components for linear networks and Fourier modes for convolutional networks. It derives both the generated distribution and its KL divergence throughout training. The resulting spectral bias has a precise form: the time needed for a mode to converge follows an inverse power law of its variance, so higher-variance modes converge faster.

Experiments on Gaussian data and natural images find that this power-law pattern remains robust with deeper or convolutional architectures. The exact solutions apply to the specified simplified settings, while the experiments support a broader empirical pattern. Together, the findings suggest how data covariance shapes learning order and offer a possible explanation for incorrect image details when training stops early.
neurips-2025-an-analytical-theory-of-spe.tldr: Exact analyses of simplified diffusion denoisers reveal variance-dependent learning speeds, with related spectral bias observed in broader experiments.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether large-scale pretraining overcomes known transformer limitations or mainly strengthens particular abilities within those limits. It studies retrieval and copying tasks, using a theoretical framework that supplies guarantees about length generalization for the settings considered. Length generalization concerns whether a learned behavior continues to work on longer sequences.

The experiments reveal a directional imbalance: pretrained models retrieve tokens to the right of a query token more successfully than tokens to its left. The authors call these behaviors induction and anti-induction. Targeted fine-tuning removes the imbalance in settings where theory guarantees length generalization, connecting the effects of training to the underlying task structure.

Mechanistic analysis links the imbalance to differences in the strength of the corresponding internal circuits. Experiments on real-world tasks also demonstrate reliability risks associated with the findings. The overall conclusion is that pretraining selectively develops transformer capabilities without removing fundamental limits on length generalization. This distinguishes a capability that fine-tuning can strengthen from an architectural restriction that pretraining has not resolved.
neurips-2025-born-a-transformer-always-a.tldr: Pretraining favors some transformer retrieval behaviors, while targeted fine-tuning corrects observed asymmetries only in the theoretically supported settings studied.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply language models with structured external information, but complex queries require retrieval that is both relevant and diverse. Supervising every intermediate retrieval decision is expensive. GraphFlow addresses this problem by learning how to navigate text-rich graphs using rewards attached to retrieval outcomes.

Its training objective jointly learns a retrieval policy and a flow estimator. The estimator distributes an outcome's reward across intermediate retrieval states, giving the policy guidance about which choices lead toward useful information. The policy is trained to retrieve candidates in proportion to their reward, encouraging exploration of multiple promising graph regions rather than relying on a single retrieval route.

On STaRK, a benchmark containing real-world queries across several domains, GraphFlow exceeds strong knowledge-graph retrieval baselines, including GPT-4o, by an average of 10% in hit rate and recall. It also shows strong generalization to unseen graphs. These results support the usefulness of learning intermediate retrieval guidance from outcome rewards when the objective is to return varied, relevant knowledge.
neurips-2025-can-knowledge-graph-based-r.tldr: GraphFlow learns reward-guided graph retrieval that improves relevance and diversity without relying on costly supervision for every retrieval step.

paragraphs: A model can produce or repair code successfully without an evaluation revealing how well it understands the program's internal relationships. CoRe examines that understanding directly through static analysis tasks. These tasks focus on how values propagate, how control decisions affect execution, and how information moves between program elements.

The human-verified benchmark contains 12,553 instances covering data dependency, control dependency, and information flow in C/C++, Java, and Python. Its sampling strategy considers program structure and dependency depth when choosing instances. This gives the evaluation semantic variety while including relationships that require following multiple steps, rather than concentrating only on readily visible connections.

Across ten evaluated language models, dependency identification is comparatively successful, but deeper semantic reasoning remains challenging. Qualitative analysis identifies complex control structures and backward dependency patterns as particular difficulties. The benchmark therefore provides a more focused view of code understanding than end-to-end success alone: it helps distinguish recognizing a dependency from reasoning through the chain of program behavior that establishes it.
neurips-2025-core-benchmarking-llms-code.tldr: CoRe tests program dependencies and information flow directly, revealing weaknesses in language models' deeper, multi-step code reasoning.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible image, molecule, or biological sequence is different from generating one that also performs well under a desired reward. This paper tackles the problem of improving that reward while preserving the natural design space learned by a diffusion model. Existing approaches often require differentiable predictors or expensive changes to the generator.

The proposed method instead modifies sampling from a pretrained model. It uses soft value functions to assess how intermediate noisy states may lead to rewarding outcomes later. Incorporating this look-ahead information into iterative generation guides the process without fine-tuning the diffusion model or constructing a differentiable reward model.

That design allows direct use of reward feedback and features that do not provide derivatives, which is useful for the scientific applications considered. It also provides a principled way to guide discrete diffusion models. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in image, molecule, and DNA/RNA generation. The contribution is a shared sampling approach for these settings, connecting downstream objectives to generation through predictions of future reward.
neurips-2025-derivative-free-guidance-in.tldr: Soft value functions guide pretrained diffusion sampling toward rewarding outcomes without generator fine-tuning or differentiable reward models.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts a generative model through low-rank updates, reducing the number of parameters that need training. The paper examines why increasing the rank does not reliably improve accuracy. It reports that performance often stagnates or declines beyond the most effective rank range, and attributes this behavior to a structural bottleneck that entangles gradients from unrelated input channels.

GraLoRA changes how the adaptation is organized. It divides weight matrices into smaller blocks and gives each block its own low-rank adapter. This more granular structure is designed to improve gradient propagation and increase representational capacity, bringing adaptation behavior closer to full fine-tuning with negligible computational or storage cost.

Experiments cover code generation, several forms of language reasoning and understanding, and image generation. GraLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and other evaluated baselines, with gains reaching 8.5 percentage points in HumanEval+ Pass@1. Improvements across model sizes and rank settings support the idea that the organization of adapter capacity matters alongside its size, rather than assuming that a wider shared bottleneck will suffice.
neurips-2025-gralora-granular-low-rank-a.tldr: GraLoRA assigns separate low-rank adapters to weight sub-blocks, improving fine-tuning performance by addressing gradient entanglement in standard LoRA.

paragraphs: GUI-G1 studies how reinforcement learning should be adapted to locating interface elements on a screen. The authors examine input templates, rewards, and policy updates in pipelines that ask models to reason before predicting a location. Their analyses find that longer reasoning chains coincide with worse grounding, some rewards can be exploited through box size, and training favors easier examples.

The proposed changes address these issues individually. A direct-answer template reduces excessive reasoning during training. A box-size constraint discourages reward exploitation that produces poor localization. Adjustments to length normalization and difficulty-dependent scaling change the learning objective so that harder samples receive better optimization.

Using 17,000 public samples and Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, the resulting GUI-G1-3B reaches 90.3% accuracy on ScreenSpot and 37.1% on ScreenSpot-Pro. It exceeds prior similarly sized models and the larger UI-TARS-7B in the reported comparisons. The findings show why training choices successful in general reasoning need task-specific examination when the required output is a precise visual location.
neurips-2025-gui-g1-understanding-r1-zer.tldr: GUI-G1 improves interface grounding by shortening training responses, constraining box-based rewards, and giving harder examples better optimization.

paragraphs: Images taken from above water can be distorted as light passes through its moving surface. This paper seeks to recover the underlying image by modeling how the surface changes across a sequence. Its key assumption is that the scene being viewed remains constant while the water produces different distortions over time.

The method uses two neural fields. One predicts surface height at each position and time; the other predicts the underlying image's color at each position. Together, they reconstruct the observed image sequence. Training can therefore use the observations themselves as the reconstruction target, allowing the model to learn without supervised image-restoration examples.

The authors find that SIREN networks, which use periodic activation functions, effectively represent both the changing surface height and the derivatives needed for image reconstruction. Tests on simulated and real data outperform the latest unsupervised restoration approach in the reported comparison. The method also estimates the water surface, connecting image recovery to an explicit account of the physical distortion that produced the observations.
neurips-2025-looking-into-the-water-by-u.tldr: Two neural fields jointly recover a constant underwater image and a changing water surface by reconstructing observed distorted frames.

paragraphs: MMMG evaluates whether image generators can create informative visuals such as diagrams, charts, and mind maps. These images must represent facts and relationships clearly, requiring world knowledge to be translated into visual content. The benchmark contains 4,456 expert-validated image-prompt pairs across ten disciplines and six educational levels.

To make the intended content explicit, the authors represent each target image with a knowledge graph of its core entities and dependencies. MMMG-Score combines factual fidelity, measured through graph-edit distance between knowledge graphs, with an assessment of visual clarity. This connects evaluation to both what the image communicates and how clearly it communicates it.

Testing 21 image-generation models reveals problems with entity fidelity, relationships, and clutter. GPT-4o scores 50.20, illustrating the benchmark's difficulty. The authors also release FLUX-Reason, an open baseline combining a reasoning language model with diffusion models, trained on 16,000 curated pairs and scoring 34.45. Together, the benchmark and baseline make explanatory image generation a concrete target for evaluating multimodal reasoning.
neurips-2025-mmmg-a-massive-multidiscipl.tldr: MMMG evaluates factual structure and visual clarity in knowledge-image generation, exposing substantial reasoning weaknesses across 21 models.

paragraphs: Vehicle routing has multiple task variants, making a single solver that generalizes across them appealing. The paper identifies a training obstacle: existing reinforcement-learning approaches to multi-task routing are limited to lightweight decoders and small problems, with weaker generalization to larger instances. MTL-KD aims to train a more capable shared decoder efficiently.

The method transfers policy knowledge from several reinforcement-learning models, each trained for one task, into a single heavier decoder. This knowledge-distillation setup enables label-free training while combining expertise across routing tasks. The authors also introduce Random Reordering Re-Construction, an inference strategy designed to work flexibly across different vehicle-routing variants and improve the shared model's solutions.

Evaluation covers six seen and ten unseen variants, with problems containing up to 1,000 nodes. The method consistently achieves superior performance in the reported uniform and real-world benchmark comparisons. These results support the use of specialist policies as training guidance for a general solver, with evidence of transfer both to unfamiliar task variants and to larger routing problems.
neurips-2025-mtl-kd-multi-task-learning-.tldr: MTL-KD distills specialist routing policies into a larger shared decoder that generalizes across seen and unseen vehicle-routing variants.

paragraphs: NavBench examines whether multimodal language models can understand navigation situations and carry out movement decisions in a zero-shot setting. It separates navigation comprehension from step-by-step execution, allowing evaluation of both interpreting a task and acting through it. This targets embodied abilities that are not fully captured by general vision-language performance.

The comprehension component contains 3,200 question-answer pairs covering instruction alignment, progress estimation, and reasoning from local observations to actions. Execution is assessed through 432 episodes across 72 indoor scenes, organized by spatial, cognitive, and execution complexity. A supporting pipeline translates model outputs into robotic actions, connecting the evaluation to deployment-oriented use.

GPT-4o performs well across tasks, while lighter open-source models succeed in simpler situations. Higher comprehension scores tend to accompany stronger execution, and map context improves decision accuracy, especially at medium difficulty. Most models nevertheless struggle to judge temporal progress. This identifies tracking how far a navigation task has advanced as a particular challenge alongside understanding instructions and immediate surroundings.
neurips-2025-navbench-probing-multimodal.tldr: NavBench evaluates navigation understanding and execution, finding useful map benefits but widespread difficulty estimating progress over time.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes the emergence of simple feature structures near the output of a trained neural network. Earlier theoretical explanations often treated those features as freely adjustable variables, then showed that globally optimal solutions possess the desired structure. That approach leaves open how actual network computations and training dynamics produce it.

This paper proves neural collapse for gradient-flow training of a two-layer ReLU classifier on orthogonally separable data. The features are therefore generated by a nonlinear network operating on structured inputs, rather than optimized independently. Gradient flow supplies the training dynamics in the theorem, connecting the result to how parameters change during learning.

The result advances the explanation in two related ways. It incorporates the effects of data structure and nonlinear activation functions, and it identifies the implicit bias of training dynamics as a contributor to collapse. The guarantee is tied to the shallow architecture, gradient-flow setting, and stated data condition. Within that setting, it explains emergence during training rather than only describing the geometry of global minima.
neurips-2025-neural-collapse-under-gradi.tldr: The paper proves neural collapse under gradient flow for two-layer ReLU classifiers with orthogonally separable data.

paragraphs: Extra computation during generation can improve diffusion-model outputs, but repeatedly optimizing each sample's starting noise makes inference slower. This paper asks whether the benefits of that optimization can be learned during post-training. Its goal is to retain much of the quality improvement while reducing the computation required for each new generation.

The proposed Noise Hypernetwork modulates the initial noise supplied to a distilled generator. Instead of performing reward-guided noise optimization at test time, the network learns a noise distribution that favors desired outcomes. A theoretically grounded, tractable objective operates in noise space and balances the desired characteristics with fidelity to the base model.

The reported results recover a substantial portion of explicit test-time optimization's quality gains at a fraction of its computational cost. The claim is therefore about retaining much of the benefit, rather than reproducing every gain. The approach illustrates how a repeated inference-time search can be partly absorbed into a learned component, shifting work into post-training while keeping generation comparatively efficient.
neurips-2025-noise-hypernetworks-amortiz.tldr: Noise Hypernetworks learn to shape diffusion inputs, recovering much of reward-guided noise optimization's quality improvement with lower inference cost.

paragraphs: Pansharpening combines high-resolution panchromatic imagery with lower-resolution multispectral observations to recover images with both spatial detail and spectral information. PINO approaches this fusion through the physical process by which a sensor records light. Its aim is to make the reconstructed image consistent with the sensor's imaging mechanism.

A pair of encoders first gathers spatial and spectral features at multiple levels of detail. An iterative neural integral process then uses the combined features to learn a continuous radiance field over location and wavelength. Finally, the sensor's wavelength-dependent response modulates that field to produce the fused image, explicitly connecting the representation of light to the recorded spectral bands.

Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show improvements over state-of-the-art fusion methods, including fewer spectral distortions and finer spatial textures. An extension to hyperspectral data supplies additional evidence of generalization. The contribution is a fusion framework in which spectral integration and sensor response help organize the reconstruction, tying improved visual detail to the preservation of meaningful spectral information.
neurips-2025-physics-informed-neural-ope.tldr: PINO models radiance and sensor response to fuse spatial and spectral imagery with improved detail and reduced spectral distortion.

paragraphs: Supervised visualization uses expert labels to guide how data are represented, with the goal of making structure understandable rather than only predicting classes. RF-PHATE advances this goal through random forests and geometric modeling, but lacks an explicit mapping for new observations. That makes scaling and use with unseen data more difficult.

Random Forest Autoencoders address this gap by learning a neural mapping that extends the representation beyond the original samples. The framework combines autoencoders with the supervision supplied by random forests and the geometry captured by RF-PHATE. In this way, the learned network carries an existing label-guided geometric representation over to additional data.

The authors report efficient visualization of unseen samples and improvements in accuracy and interpretability over existing approaches, including RF-PHATE's standard kernel extension. They also report robustness to hyperparameter choices and applicability to any kernel-based dimensionality-reduction method. The main practical contribution is an explicit extension mechanism, making guided representations more usable when observations arrive after the initial visualization has been constructed.
neurips-2025-random-forest-autoencoders-.tldr: Random Forest Autoencoders learn an explicit mapping that extends label-guided visualizations efficiently to unseen data.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can lose image quality when asked to generate beyond the resolution used during training. ScaleDiff addresses this without additional training, while targeting the computational cost and architectural compatibility problems of earlier approaches. It is designed to work with pretrained models built around either U-Nets or Diffusion Transformers.

Its central attention mechanism, Neighborhood Patch Attention, uses non-overlapping patches to reduce redundant self-attention computation. The framework incorporates this mechanism into an SDEdit pipeline. Latent Frequency Mixing helps generate fine detail, while Structure Guidance supports the overall arrangement of the image during denoising. These components address local detail and global structure alongside inference efficiency.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art image quality and inference speed among training-free methods on both architecture families. This matters because extending resolution requires more than simply producing a larger image: the method also has to preserve coherent structure and useful detail. ScaleDiff's results support combining attention efficiency with separate mechanisms for fine-scale content and global organization.
neurips-2025-scalediff-higher-resolution.tldr: ScaleDiff extends pretrained diffusion models to higher resolutions without training, combining efficient attention with detail and structure guidance.

paragraphs: SCOUT explores reasoning through repeated internal computation rather than depending on manually supervised intermediate reasoning steps. Its underlying Flow Chain-of-Thought framework treats recursive inference as a progression of latent cognitive states. Each iteration is intended to develop the reasoning further, giving repeated computation an explicit learning structure.

The method enables this behavior through lightweight fine-tuning of pretrained language models. Progressive distillation aligns successive iterations with teachers of appropriate capacity. A retrospective module uses cross-attention to incorporate outputs from earlier iterations while preserving the model's original computation flow. Together, these mechanisms provide guidance about how reasoning should develop and how previous iterations should inform later ones.

Across eight reasoning benchmarks, SCOUT consistently improves accuracy and explanation quality, with reported fine-tuning gains of up to 1.8%. Qualitative analyses also show progressively refined beliefs and more detailed explanations across iterations. These findings support the practical usefulness of training a structured progression of internal reasoning, without requiring a new pretraining stage or manual supervision of each reasoning step.
neurips-2025-scout-teaching-pre-trained-.tldr: SCOUT uses progressive teacher distillation and retrospective attention to improve recursive reasoning through lightweight fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Understanding a model's visual representations is easier when individual features correspond to recognizable concepts. This paper studies whether sparse autoencoders can improve that property, called monosemanticity, in vision-language models such as CLIP. It extends an interpretability approach previously applied to language models into the visual representation setting.

The authors introduce a neuron-level evaluation framework and build a benchmark from a large-scale user study so that the assessment reflects human perception. Their experiments find that sparse autoencoders substantially improve the monosemanticity of individual neurons. Sparsity and wide latent representations are the most influential factors in the reported results, connecting the autoencoder's design to how interpretable its features become.

The work also demonstrates control: interventions through the autoencoder on CLIP's vision encoder steer outputs from multimodal language models such as LLaVA without modifying the language model itself. This connects visual feature interpretation to an actionable intervention point. The results support sparse autoencoders as an unsupervised tool for both inspecting and influencing vision-language systems.
neurips-2025-sparse-autoencoders-learn-m.tldr: Sparse autoencoders make vision-language features more interpretable and enable output steering through interventions in the vision encoder.

paragraphs: Models trained for object recognition have helped explain neuronal activity in the primate visual system's ventral stream. Comparable modeling of the dorsal stream, associated with spatial relationships and motion, has been held back by limited datasets. STSBench addresses that gap by providing substantially more neural recordings during natural video viewing.

The dataset contains single-neuron recordings from more than 2,000 neurons in the superior temporal sulcus of rhesus macaques watching thousands of distinct natural videos. The authors describe its scale as nearly fifty times that of existing dorsal-stream datasets. This pairs varied visual input with measured neuronal responses, providing material for studying how the recorded areas represent visual information.

The paper demonstrates two uses: benchmarking models that predict neuronal responses and reconstructing visual input from neural activity. These directions examine the relationship between videos and responses from opposite sides. STSBench's contribution is therefore both a larger empirical resource and a basis for evaluating models of a visual-processing stream whose computational characterization remains less developed.
neurips-2025-stsbench-a-large-scale-data.tldr: STSBench provides large-scale primate neural recordings during natural video viewing for response prediction and visual reconstruction.

paragraphs: Object detectors may encounter new visual conditions and object categories after deployment. This paper develops test-time adaptation around a foundation vision-language detector, removing the need for source data and the requirement that training and target categories match. The approach updates the model using incoming test observations.

A multimodal mean-teacher framework tunes both text and visual prompts, adapting the language and vision representations with relatively few parameters. A warm-start strategy for visual prompts helps preserve the vision branch's representational capability. An Instance Dynamic Memory stores high-quality pseudo-labels from earlier test samples, making useful past predictions available during later adaptation.

Two memory-based strategies improve current predictions and support images without available pseudo-labels. This combines parameter-efficient adaptation with an effort to maintain useful supervision across test batches. Experiments on cross-corruption and cross-dataset benchmarks consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. The reported results support adaptation across changes in both domain and category space, addressing the closed-category restriction that limits traditional approaches.
neurips-2025-test-time-adaptive-object-d.tldr: A foundation detector adapts at test time through multimodal prompts and pseudo-label memory without source data or matching category sets.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce portions of their training data exactly, and many proposed defenses require retraining or access to model weights. TokenSwap targets a more restricted deployment setting where users have access only to token-level outputs. It aims to interrupt memorized sequences while retaining the capabilities that make a large model useful.

The method draws on a division of labor between large and small models. Large models supply strong task performance, while smaller models can assign fluent probabilities to common function words and memorize much less. TokenSwap selectively exchanges token probabilities between the models, changing parts of generation where a smaller model can provide grammatically plausible guidance.

Evaluations on Pythia-6.9B and Llama-3-8B show reductions in exact memorization of up to a factor of ten, with negligible task degradation. These are measured reductions, rather than a guarantee that memorized text cannot appear. The contribution is a lightweight post-hoc intervention that uses token probabilities to disrupt verbatim reproduction without requiring changes to the large model's internal weights.
neurips-2025-tokenswap-a-lightweight-met.tldr: TokenSwap selectively substitutes small-model token probabilities to reduce verbatim memorization while largely preserving tested task performance.

paragraphs: Directly observing how tau pathology spreads through the living brain is difficult. This paper seeks to infer meaningful spreading pathways between two longitudinal scans, while modeling interaction with amyloid-beta burden. It uses a physics-informed learning framework based on a prion-like account of propagation.

The authors formulate tau spreading as a mean-field game: behavior at each location depends on surrounding locations and an amyloid-related potential field. Under the governing dynamics, equilibrium provides an optimal-transport description of tau evolution. A Wasserstein-1 Lagrangian generative adversarial network learns this transport, with a critic estimating appropriate population-level transport costs and a generator representing individual flow fields.

A symbolic regression module additionally produces an explicit expression for amyloid-beta–tau interaction, connecting the learned dynamics to an interpretable formulation. On public neuroimaging datasets, the model yields precise and reliable predictions of future tau progression for previously unseen subjects. The results support the framework as a way to study possible propagation mechanisms through learned pathways and equations, alongside its predictive use.
neurips-2025-uncover-governing-law-of-pa.tldr: A mean-field-game model learns tau propagation pathways and an explicit amyloid–tau relationship from longitudinal brain imaging.

paragraphs: VideoVLA investigates whether pretrained video generators can provide a useful foundation for robot manipulation. Given a language instruction and an image, it predicts both a sequence of actions and the future visual outcomes. This connects the robot's proposed behavior to an imagined account of what that behavior will look like.

The system uses a multimodal Diffusion Transformer to model video, language, and actions together. Pretrained video-generation capability supports joint visual and action forecasting. The central design choice is to learn these predictions together, bringing the ability to anticipate visual change into the same framework that produces manipulation actions.

Experiments find that higher-quality imagined futures correlate with more reliable action predictions and greater task success. They also show strong generalization, including handling unfamiliar objects and imitating skills from other embodiments. The correlation supports the relevance of visual forecasting without by itself establishing that better imagery causes successful manipulation. Overall, the findings support joint prediction of actions and consequences as a promising route to more generalizable robotic behavior.
neurips-2025-videovla-video-generators-c.tldr: VideoVLA jointly predicts robot actions and future video, showing generalization to novel objects and skills from other embodiments.
